notes: Initial Version 2 bank: 300 original practice items, 50 per subject, with option-by-option rationales.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Which crop is a classic C4 plant and is generally more efficient than C3 crops under high light, high temperature, and limited CO₂ conditions?
questions.explanation: Maize uses the C4 pathway, concentrating CO₂ around Rubisco and reducing photorespiration under hot, bright conditions.
optionExplanations: Rice is a C3 crop and has greater photorespiration under hot conditions.
Correct. Maize is a C4 crop with Kranz anatomy and efficient CO₂ concentration.
Potato is a C3 crop.
Soybean is a C3 legume.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A short-day plant flowers when:
options: Day length exceeds a critical maximum
Night length is shorter than a critical minimum
The uninterrupted night is longer than a critical duration
questions.explanation: For many short-day plants, the critical signal is a sufficiently long, uninterrupted dark period.
optionExplanations: Long days generally favor long-day plants, not short-day plants.
Short nights tend to inhibit flowering of short-day plants.
Correct. A long uninterrupted night is the key photoperiodic requirement.
Low temperature may affect vernalization but does not define short-day response.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Which plant hormone is most directly associated with fruit ripening and abscission in many crops?
questions.explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that promotes climacteric fruit ripening and can promote senescence and abscission.
optionExplanations: Auxin is strongly associated with cell elongation, apical dominance, and rooting.
Correct. Ethylene regulates ripening, senescence, and abscission.
Cytokinins promote cell division and delay senescence in many tissues.
Gibberellins promote stem elongation, bolting, and seed germination.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A seed with high viability but low vigor is most likely to:
options: Germinate well under ideal conditions but perform poorly under field stress
Always produce higher yield than high-vigor seed
questions.explanation: Viability is the ability to germinate, while vigor reflects rapid, uniform establishment especially under suboptimal field conditions.
optionExplanations: Low-vigor seed can still pass a standard germination test.
Correct. Vigor differences often appear under stress rather than ideal laboratory conditions.
A seed with no living embryo is nonviable.
Low vigor does not guarantee high yield.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A farmer plants 20,000 hills per hectare with two plants per hill. What is the plant population per hectare?
questions.explanation: Plant population = hills per hectare × plants per hill = 20,000 × 2 = 40,000 plants/ha.
optionExplanations: This divides instead of multiplying.
This counts hills, not individual plants.
Correct. 20,000 × 2 = 40,000 plants/ha.
This would require four plants per hill.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Heterosis refers to:
options: The loss of vigor due to crossing
Superior performance of an F1 hybrid relative to its parents
Fixation of all loci in a population
questions.explanation: Heterosis or hybrid vigor is the enhanced performance of a hybrid compared with the parental lines for one or more traits.
optionExplanations: This describes inbreeding depression rather than heterosis.
Correct. F1 hybrids may exceed the average or even the better parent.
Repeated selfing increases homozygosity.
Fixation is not the definition of heterosis.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Which breeding method is most appropriate for improving a highly self-pollinated crop while recovering most characteristics of an elite variety and adding one specific gene?
questions.explanation: Backcrossing repeatedly crosses progeny to the recurrent elite parent while selecting for a desired donor gene.
optionExplanations: Mass selection improves populations but is less precise for transferring one gene.
Correct. Backcrossing is designed to transfer a specific trait into an established genotype.
Recurrent selection is especially common in cross-pollinated populations.
Synthetic varieties are made from selected intercrossing lines or clones, usually in cross-pollinated crops.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Which is an advantage of vegetative propagation?
options: It always creates greater genetic variability
It maintains the genotype of a desirable clone
questions.explanation: Vegetative propagation preserves the genotype of the parent and is useful for clonally maintained crops.
optionExplanations: Sexual reproduction generally creates more genetic variation.
Correct. Clonal propagation maintains genetically identical material except for mutation.
Viruses and other systemic pathogens may also be propagated.
Many vegetatively propagated plants do not develop a true seed-derived taproot.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same field without a distinct row arrangement is called:
questions.explanation: Mixed cropping involves simultaneous growth of more than one crop without a definite spatial arrangement.
optionExplanations: Relay cropping introduces the next crop before the first crop is harvested.
Correct. Mixed cropping has no distinct row arrangement.
Sequential cropping grows crops one after another in time.
Monocropping uses only one crop.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Temporary midday wilting on a hot day can occur even when soil moisture is adequate because:
options: Transpiration temporarily exceeds root water uptake
Stomata are fully open all night
questions.explanation: Midday wilting can occur when atmospheric demand causes water loss to exceed the rate at which roots can replace it.
optionExplanations: Correct. A temporary water deficit can develop in leaves even with moist soil.
Root respiration does not permanently stop during midday heat.
Night stomatal behavior does not explain midday wilting.
Xylem and phloem do not convert into each other.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: For a climacteric fruit intended for distant markets, the most appropriate harvest strategy is generally to harvest:
options: Only after complete softening on the plant
At physiological/mature-green stage before full eating ripeness
Only after seeds begin germinating inside the fruit
questions.explanation: Climacteric fruits can continue ripening after harvest, so mature-green harvest can improve transportability and shelf life.
optionExplanations: Fully soft fruit is more susceptible to handling damage.
Correct. Mature-green fruit can complete ripening after harvest.
Fruit harvested immediately after flowering is immature.
Seed germination inside the fruit is not a harvest maturity standard.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Harvest index is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Harvest index expresses the proportion of total biological production that becomes the economic product.
optionExplanations: Correct. HI = economic yield / biological yield, often expressed as a percentage.
This is the inverse of harvest index.
Root-to-leaf ratio is a different growth parameter.
Seed rate is not the denominator of harvest index.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Which visual symptom most strongly suggests nitrogen deficiency in many crops?
options: Older leaves become generally chlorotic first
Young leaves show interveinal chlorosis first
Leaf margins burn first while veins remain green
Growing points die first with distorted young leaves
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile in plants, so deficiency symptoms commonly appear first on older leaves as general chlorosis.
optionExplanations: Correct. Mobile N is remobilized from old to young leaves.
Young-leaf interveinal chlorosis is more typical of immobile micronutrient deficiencies such as iron.
Marginal scorch can be associated with potassium deficiency.
Death of growing points and distorted young tissue can be associated with calcium or boron problems.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: The critical period of weed control is best described as the:
options: Time when weeds must be completely absent for the entire season
Crop growth interval during which weeds must be controlled to prevent unacceptable yield loss
Period after harvest when weeds have no effect
Time when only perennial weeds germinate
questions.explanation: The critical period is the window in crop development when weed competition must be minimized to protect yield.
optionExplanations: Season-long zero weeds may be unnecessary and uneconomical.
Correct. Timely control during this window prevents economically important yield loss.
Postharvest weeds can still affect future seedbanks, and this is not the definition.
It is not limited to perennial weed germination.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Closing stomata during drought conserves water but directly reduces:
questions.explanation: Stomatal closure reduces transpiration but also limits diffusion of CO₂ into leaves, lowering photosynthetic carbon assimilation.
optionExplanations: Correct. Reduced CO₂ entry is a key trade-off of stomatal closure.
Drought can affect chlorophyll, but stomatal closure does not directly reduce it to zero.
Root anchorage is structural and not the direct effect.
Genetic purity is unrelated.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: The plant disease triangle requires a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen, and:
questions.explanation: Disease develops when a susceptible host, a capable pathogen, and favorable environmental conditions coincide over sufficient time.
optionExplanations: Correct. Environment is the third classic component.
Pesticide residue is not required for disease.
Pollinators are not part of the disease triangle.
Fertility may influence susceptibility but is not the third defining component.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Which practice most directly reduces primary inoculum of a residue-borne plant pathogen?
options: Sanitation and destruction of infected crop debris
questions.explanation: Removing or destroying infected residues reduces the amount of pathogen inoculum available to initiate disease.
optionExplanations: Correct. Sanitation targets the initial inoculum source.
Dense planting often increases humidity and disease risk.
Night irrigation can prolong leaf wetness.
Excess nitrogen can make some crops more susceptible.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: An insect with egg–larva–pupa–adult development undergoes:
questions.explanation: Complete metamorphosis (holometaboly) includes distinct larval and pupal stages before the adult.
optionExplanations: Ametabolous insects lack true metamorphosis.
Incomplete metamorphosis is egg–nymph–adult and lacks a pupa.
Correct. Egg–larva–pupa–adult is complete metamorphosis.
Paedogenesis is reproduction by immature forms in some organisms.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Rice stem borers are difficult to control with contact insecticides after larvae enter the stem mainly because:
options: The larvae are physically protected inside plant tissue
questions.explanation: Once larvae bore into the stem, plant tissue shields them from direct contact with many surface-applied insecticides.
optionExplanations: Correct. Concealed feeding limits spray contact.
Larvae do not instantly become adults.
They continue feeding within the stem.
Insecticides do not become fertilizers.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: The best description of integrated pest management (IPM) is:
options: Routine calendar spraying regardless of pest density
Combining compatible tactics and using pesticides judiciously based on monitoring and thresholds
Eliminating every insect species in the field
questions.explanation: IPM integrates cultural, biological, physical, genetic, and chemical tools while considering economics, ecology, and pest monitoring.
optionExplanations: Calendar spraying can be wasteful and disrupt natural enemies.
Correct. IPM combines compatible methods and informed decision-making.
Eradication of all insects is neither realistic nor desirable.
Biological control is one IPM component, not the whole system.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: In IPM, the economic threshold is the pest density at which:
options: Crop damage has already exceeded total crop value
Control action should be taken to prevent the pest from reaching the economic injury level
questions.explanation: The economic threshold is an action point set below the economic injury level so control can prevent economically damaging loss.
optionExplanations: The threshold is intended to prevent losses from reaching that point.
Correct. Management begins before the economic injury level is reached.
It does not mean pesticides are ineffective.
Natural enemies are usually conserved, not destroyed.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Repeated use of one insecticide mode of action can rapidly select resistance because:
options: Resistant individuals survive and contribute more offspring to the next generation
The insecticide changes the crop into a pest
All mutations are caused by the insecticide
questions.explanation: Resistance evolves by selection: rare resistant genotypes survive treatment and become more frequent over generations.
optionExplanations: Susceptible insects are preferentially killed, not favored.
Correct. Survivors pass resistance alleles to descendants.
The crop does not become a pest.
Mutations can arise independently; insecticide use mainly selects existing or new resistance variants.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: A selective herbicide is one that:
options: Controls certain weeds at labeled rates while the crop tolerates the treatment
questions.explanation: Selectivity allows control of target weeds without unacceptable injury to the crop under proper use conditions.
optionExplanations: That describes a nonselective effect.
Correct. Selective herbicides exploit physiological, biochemical, placement, or timing differences.
Fungicides target fungi.
All pesticides have use restrictions and safety requirements.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Why is preventing weed seed production an important long-term control strategy?
options: It reduces additions to the soil weed seedbank
It makes all herbicides unnecessary immediately
questions.explanation: Stopping seed rain reduces future weed recruitment and gradually depletes the seedbank when combined with other controls.
optionExplanations: Correct. Fewer new seeds means lower future infestation pressure.
The objective is not to increase diversity.
Soil is not sterilized by preventing seed production.
Other control tactics may still be needed.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Koch's postulates are primarily used to:
options: Prove a causal relationship between a suspected pathogen and a disease
questions.explanation: Koch's postulates provide a classical framework for associating a microorganism with a specific disease through isolation, inoculation, symptom reproduction, and re-isolation.
optionExplanations: Correct. They are used to establish disease causation.
Fertilizer efficiency is an agronomic calculation.
Soil texture is determined from particle-size distribution.
Market price is an economic outcome.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Root-knot nematodes commonly cause:
options: Powdery growth on leaf surfaces only
questions.explanation: Meloidogyne species induce characteristic root galls that disrupt water and nutrient uptake.
optionExplanations: Correct. Root galling is a classic symptom.
Powdery leaf growth suggests powdery mildew fungi.
Chewed holes suggest insect feeding.
Bacterial ooze may occur in bacterial diseases but is not typical of root-knot nematodes.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Moko disease of banana is caused by a bacterium in the Ralstonia solanacearum species complex. Which action is most appropriate in an infested field?
options: Use clean planting material and promptly destroy infected mats while disinfecting tools
Move contaminated soil to clean farms
questions.explanation: Moko management relies heavily on exclusion, sanitation, removal of infected plants, tool disinfection, and avoiding movement of contaminated material.
optionExplanations: Correct. Sanitation and clean planting material reduce spread.
Symptomatic mats can carry the pathogen.
Moving contaminated soil spreads inoculum.
Extra overhead irrigation can aid splash and movement of some pathogens and is not a control measure.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: A fungicide that remains mainly on the plant surface and protects tissue before infection is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Protectant fungicides act primarily on the surface and are most effective when applied before infection.
optionExplanations: Correct. Contact protectants prevent infection on treated surfaces.
Systemic fungicides are absorbed and translocated to varying degrees.
Herbicides control weeds.
Rodenticides control rodents.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: A parasitoid differs from a typical predator because a parasitoid:
options: Usually develops on or in a single host and ultimately kills it
Consumes many prey individuals during its lifetime
questions.explanation: Parasitoids generally require one host for immature development and eventually kill that host; predators typically consume multiple prey.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the defining parasitoid relationship.
That is more typical of predators.
Many parasitoids are insects such as wasps and flies.
Successful parasitoid development usually kills the host.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: When mixing and applying pesticides, the most defensible principle is to:
options: Follow the current label, use required PPE, and observe re-entry and pre-harvest intervals
Double the labeled rate to ensure control
Mix products even when compatibility is unknown
questions.explanation: The pesticide label is a legal and technical use document; PPE and interval requirements protect applicators, workers, consumers, and the environment.
optionExplanations: Correct. Label directions and protective measures are fundamental.
Exceeding labeled rates can be illegal, unsafe, phytotoxic, and accelerate resistance.
Unknown mixtures may be incompatible or unsafe.
Heat does not justify removing required PPE.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Which master horizon is usually characterized by accumulation of organic matter at the mineral soil surface and is commonly designated as topsoil?
questions.explanation: The A horizon is a mineral surface horizon commonly enriched with organic matter and biological activity.
optionExplanations: Correct. A is the typical mineral topsoil horizon.
B is commonly a zone of subsurface accumulation or alteration.
C is relatively weakly altered parent material.
R is hard bedrock.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Soil texture is determined by the relative proportions of:
questions.explanation: Texture is the particle-size composition of the fine-earth fraction: sand, silt, and clay.
optionExplanations: Correct. These three separates define texture classes.
These components affect soil condition but do not define texture.
N-P-K are nutrients, not particle-size separates.
Air, water, and microbes are not the basis of textural class.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil has a dry mass of 130 g occupying a total volume of 100 cm³. Its bulk density is:
questions.explanation: Bulk density = oven-dry soil mass ÷ total bulk volume = 130/100 = 1.30 g/cm³.
optionExplanations: This is approximately the inverse of the correct calculation.
Correct. 130 ÷ 100 = 1.30 g/cm³.
This is ten times too high.
This ignores the volume division.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Plant-available water is approximately the water held between:
options: Field capacity and permanent wilting point
Permanent wilting point and oven dryness
questions.explanation: Available water capacity is commonly defined as water content at field capacity minus water content at permanent wilting point.
optionExplanations: Water above field capacity drains relatively freely.
Correct. This range is the water most plants can potentially extract.
Water below permanent wilting point is largely unavailable.
Runoff and infiltration are hydrologic processes, not soil water limits.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil with high cation-exchange capacity generally has greater ability to retain:
options: Positively charged nutrient ions such as Ca²⁺ and K⁺
Nitrate only because it is an anion
questions.explanation: Negatively charged clay and organic matter surfaces hold exchangeable cations and reduce their immediate leaching.
optionExplanations: Correct. CEC concerns exchangeable cations.
Nitrate is negatively charged and is not strongly held by normal cation-exchange sites.
CEC does not describe suspension of sand.
Oxygen gas is not retained by cation exchange.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Liming an acidic mineral soil primarily aims to:
options: Raise soil pH and reduce acidity-related constraints
questions.explanation: Agricultural lime neutralizes acidity, raises pH, and can reduce toxic exchangeable Al while supplying Ca and sometimes Mg.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the main objective of liming acidic soil.
Proper liming is not intended to create salinity.
Base saturation generally increases with liming.
Exchangeable Al generally decreases as pH rises.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Nitrification is the microbial conversion of:
options: Organic N directly to N₂ gas
Ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate
Nitrate to ammonium in plant roots only
N₂ gas to ammonia by lightning only
questions.explanation: Nitrifying microorganisms oxidize ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate under generally aerobic conditions.
optionExplanations: Conversion of organic N to ammonium is mineralization; loss to N₂ is denitrification.
Correct. NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ is nitrification.
This is not the standard definition of nitrification.
Nitrogen fixation converts N₂ to reduced N forms; it is not nitrification.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Which condition most favors denitrification losses of soil nitrogen?
options: Waterlogged soil with limited oxygen and available nitrate
Dry, well-aerated sandy soil with no nitrate
Very low microbial activity under complete dryness
questions.explanation: Denitrifying microbes use nitrate as an electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions, producing gaseous N forms.
optionExplanations: Correct. Saturation and low oxygen favor denitrification.
Aerobic dry conditions do not favor denitrification.
Lack of microbes and nitrate prevents meaningful denitrification.
Complete dryness suppresses microbial denitrification.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: In strongly acidic soils, phosphorus availability can be reduced because phosphorus is fixed mainly by:
questions.explanation: At low pH, Fe and Al oxides and hydroxides strongly sorb or precipitate phosphorus, reducing plant availability.
optionExplanations: Correct. Fe and Al are major P-fixing agents in acid soils.
NaCl is not the main mechanism.
Atmospheric N is unrelated to P fixation.
Ca-related P precipitation is more important at high pH/calcareous conditions.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A sodic soil is especially associated with excessive exchangeable:
questions.explanation: High exchangeable sodium can disperse clays, degrade structure, and reduce infiltration.
optionExplanations: Correct. Exchangeable Na is the defining concern.
Calcium usually promotes flocculation rather than sodicity.
Hydrogen relates to acidity, not sodicity.
Silicon is not the defining exchangeable ion.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Increasing stable soil organic matter generally tends to:
options: Improve aggregate stability and water-holding capacity
Reduce CEC in most mineral soils
questions.explanation: Organic matter supports aggregation, nutrient retention, biological activity, and water-holding capacity.
optionExplanations: Correct. These are common benefits of soil organic matter.
Organic matter does not eliminate all pathogens.
Organic matter usually contributes to CEC rather than reducing it.
It does not transform clay particles into sand.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: On sloping cultivated land, contour farming reduces erosion primarily by:
options: Slowing downslope runoff and increasing infiltration
questions.explanation: Tillage and planting across the slope along contour lines shorten effective slope length and slow water movement.
optionExplanations: Correct. Slower runoff means less erosive energy.
Increasing slope length would generally increase erosion risk.
Direct downhill channels can accelerate erosion.
Removing residues exposes soil and may increase erosion.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A recommendation calls for 60 kg N/ha. If urea contains 46% N, approximately how much urea is needed per hectare?
questions.explanation: Required fertilizer = nutrient requirement ÷ nutrient fraction = 60 ÷ 0.46 ≈ 130.4 kg urea/ha.
optionExplanations: 27.6 kg is 46% of 60, not the amount of urea needed.
46 kg confuses percent N with fertilizer mass.
Correct. 60/0.46 ≈ 130.4 kg/ha.
276 kg would supply about 127 kg N.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Which soil structure is generally desirable in a cultivated surface horizon because it promotes good aeration and infiltration?
questions.explanation: Granular/crumb structure provides stable aggregates and connected pore spaces favorable for roots, air, and water movement.
optionExplanations: Correct. Granular structure is commonly favorable in topsoil.
Massive soil lacks natural structural units and can restrict roots.
Platy compacted structure can impede vertical movement.
Single-grain is common in sands but is not an aggregated structure.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Exchangeable aluminum becomes a major toxicity concern in many mineral soils mainly under:
options: Neutral to slightly alkaline conditions only
questions.explanation: As soil pH becomes strongly acidic, Al-bearing minerals and exchange sites can release more soluble Al³⁺, which can damage roots.
optionExplanations: Correct. Al toxicity is classically associated with strongly acid soils.
Al solubility is generally lower near neutral pH.
Salinity and acidity are different constraints.
High organic matter alone does not define Al toxicity.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: The primary site of microbial fermentation in cattle is the:
questions.explanation: The rumen houses a dense microbial community that ferments fibrous feeds to volatile fatty acids.
optionExplanations: Correct. The rumen is the major fermentation chamber.
The abomasum is the true glandular stomach.
The small intestine is a major site of enzymatic digestion and absorption.
The cecum has some fermentation but is not the primary site in cattle.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: The major energy-yielding products absorbed from rumen fermentation are:
questions.explanation: Acetate, propionate, and butyrate are the major volatile fatty acids produced by rumen microbes and supply much of a ruminant's energy.
optionExplanations: Correct. VFAs are central energy metabolites in ruminants.
Starch is largely fermented or digested before being absorbed as intact granules.
Urea participates in N recycling but is not the main energy product.
Bile salts aid fat digestion but are not fermentation energy products.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Feed conversion ratio (FCR) is commonly calculated as:
questions.explanation: FCR expresses how many units of feed are required for one unit of live-weight gain; lower values generally indicate better feed efficiency.
optionExplanations: Correct. Feed/gain is the common FCR expression.
This is gain:feed, the reciprocal efficiency measure.
Mortality is not the denominator of FCR.
Water:feed ratio is a separate management metric.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Which nutrient class is the most concentrated source of dietary energy per unit weight?
questions.explanation: Fats provide about 9 kcal/g compared with roughly 4 kcal/g for protein and carbohydrate.
optionExplanations: Correct. Fat is the most energy-dense major nutrient.
Protein can provide energy but is less energy-dense than fat.
Carbohydrate provides less energy per gram than fat.
Minerals do not provide metabolizable energy.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Ovulation in many farm mammals is triggered by a preovulatory surge of:
questions.explanation: The LH surge promotes final follicular maturation and ovulation.
optionExplanations: Correct. LH is the key ovulatory trigger.
Insulin regulates metabolism and has reproductive interactions but is not the ovulatory surge hormone.
Thyroxine regulates metabolic rate.
Prolactin is strongly associated with lactation.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Progesterone during the luteal phase is produced mainly by the:
questions.explanation: After ovulation, the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to support the uterine environment.
optionExplanations: Correct. The corpus luteum is the main luteal progesterone source.
The pituitary secretes gonadotropins such as LH and FSH.
The hypothalamus secretes GnRH.
The oviduct is primarily a transport and fertilization site.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Heritability refers to the proportion of:
options: Phenotypic variation in a population attributable to genetic variation under given conditions
An individual's traits that are caused only by genes
questions.explanation: Heritability is a population parameter describing how much observed variation is associated with genetic variation in a particular environment.
optionExplanations: Correct. It concerns variation in a population, not destiny of an individual.
Heritability does not state what fraction of one animal's trait is genetic.
Dominance is a genetic relationship, not heritability.
Survival rate is a performance measure.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: For a trait with high heritability, individual phenotypic selection is generally:
options: More effective because phenotype is a better indicator of breeding value
Impossible because genetics has little influence
questions.explanation: When heritability is high, phenotype more closely reflects genetic differences, so individual selection can be effective.
optionExplanations: Correct. Higher heritability improves accuracy of phenotypic selection.
This is the opposite of high heritability.
Sex-limited traits often require pedigree/progeny information.
Genetic response is never guaranteed at 100%.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Brooding temperature is most critical for newly hatched chicks because they:
options: Have limited ability to regulate body temperature
questions.explanation: Young chicks have immature thermoregulation and little insulation, so proper brooder temperature is essential.
optionExplanations: Correct. Chicks are highly dependent on environmental heat early in life.
Chicks can digest appropriately formulated starter feed.
They require constant access to clean water.
Newly hatched chicks lack full mature feather insulation.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Piglets are commonly given supplemental iron early in life mainly to prevent:
questions.explanation: Piglets are born with limited iron stores and sow's milk supplies little iron, so supplementation prevents anemia.
optionExplanations: Correct. Iron deficiency anemia is a classic piglet risk.
Rickets is mainly linked to vitamin D/calcium/phosphorus problems.
Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency and is not the usual issue in pigs.
Ketosis is a metabolic energy disorder, not an iron deficiency.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Which farm practice best represents external biosecurity?
options: Controlling entry of animals, people, vehicles, and equipment onto the farm
Treating a sick animal after disease spreads
Mixing newly arrived animals immediately with the herd
questions.explanation: External biosecurity aims to prevent introduction of pathogens into a farm through controlled entry and quarantine.
optionExplanations: Correct. Entry control and quarantine reduce pathogen introduction.
Treatment is disease management, not prevention of entry.
High stocking density can increase disease transmission.
New animals should usually be quarantined and assessed first.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Oxytocin is especially important in dairy animals for:
questions.explanation: Oxytocin causes contraction of myoepithelial cells around mammary alveoli, ejecting milk.
optionExplanations: Correct. Oxytocin mediates milk ejection.
Milk synthesis is more strongly supported by prolactin and metabolic hormones.
Puberty involves the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
Rumen fermentation is microbial.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A vaccine primarily protects a herd by:
options: Stimulating specific adaptive immunity before exposure or severe disease
Killing all pathogens immediately after injection
Providing unlimited lifelong immunity in every animal
questions.explanation: Vaccination primes adaptive immune responses and can reduce disease, transmission, or severity depending on the vaccine.
optionExplanations: Correct. Vaccines prepare the immune system.
Vaccines are not disinfectants or antibiotics.
Sanitation and biosecurity remain important.
Duration and effectiveness vary by vaccine, animal, and pathogen.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A broiler flock consumes 4,800 kg feed and gains 3,000 kg live weight. The FCR is:
questions.explanation: FCR = feed consumed ÷ weight gain = 4,800 ÷ 3,000 = 1.60.
optionExplanations: This is approximately the reciprocal (gain/feed).
This is too high for the calculation.
This is not derived from the given values.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Dressing percentage is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Dressing percentage indicates the proportion of live weight represented by the carcass after slaughter and dressing.
optionExplanations: Correct. Carcass/live × 100 is the standard calculation.
This is the inverse.
Feed intake is not part of dressing percentage.
Fat-to-bone ratio is a different carcass composition measure.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The value of the next best alternative forgone
Any cash payment made by a farmer
Only interest paid on a loan
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost captures the benefit sacrificed when a scarce resource is used for one alternative rather than the next best use.
optionExplanations: Correct. It includes implicit as well as explicit sacrifice.
Cash payments are explicit costs, not the full meaning of opportunity cost.
Loan interest is only one type of cost.
Fixed cost is a cost category, not opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing

Not this one. Trialability means: Degree to which an innovation can be experimented with on a limited basis before full adoption.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Which term best matches this description? “Systematic process for identifying gaps between current and desired conditions and prioritizing issues to address.”
questions.explanation: The best answer is Needs assessment. Systematic process for identifying gaps between current and desired conditions and prioritizing issues to address.
optionExplanations: Not this one. Compatibility means: Degree to which an innovation fits existing values, experiences, resources, and needs of potential adopters.
Correct. Needs assessment means: Systematic process for identifying gaps between current and desired conditions and prioritizing issues to address.
Not this one. Early majority means: Adopter category that accepts innovations before the average member but usually after deliberate consideration.
Not this one. Monitoring means: Routine or periodic tracking of inputs, activities, outputs, timelines, and immediate performance during program implementation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Which term best matches this description? “Routine or periodic tracking of inputs, activities, outputs, timelines, and immediate performance during program implementation.”
questions.explanation: The best answer is Monitoring. Routine or periodic tracking of inputs, activities, outputs, timelines, and immediate performance during program implementation.
optionExplanations: Not this one. Source means: Person, organization, or originator that encodes and sends a message.
Correct. Monitoring means: Routine or periodic tracking of inputs, activities, outputs, timelines, and immediate performance during program implementation.
Not this one. Observability means: Degree to which results of an innovation are visible or apparent to others.
Not this one. Innovator means: First adopter category; typically venturesome and willing to try new ideas despite uncertainty.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Corn is planted at 0.75 m between rows and 0.25 m between hills, one plant per hill. Ignoring border losses, approximately how many plants are established per hectare?
questions.explanation: Area per plant = 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875 m². Population = 10,000/0.1875 ≈ 53,333 plants/ha.
optionExplanations: 13,333 is far too low for the given spacing.
26,667 would correspond to roughly twice the area per plant.
75,000 would require closer spacing.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A seed lot is 95% pure seed and has 90% germination. What is its pure live seed (PLS) percentage?
questions.explanation: PLS% = purity% × germination% ÷ 100 = 95 × 90 ÷ 100 = 85.5%.
optionExplanations: Correct. 95% × 90% = 85.5% PLS.
This ignores the purity factor.
This is the arithmetic average, not PLS.
PLS cannot exceed 100% from these values.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A rice crop produces 10 t/ha total aboveground dry matter and 4 t/ha grain. Its harvest index is:
questions.explanation: Harvest index = economic yield/biological yield × 100 = 4/10 × 100 = 40%.
optionExplanations: 60% would mean 6 t grain from 10 t biomass.
A proportion of the total cannot be 250%.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A 1-ha field produces three sequential crops in one year, each occupying the full hectare. The annual cropping intensity is:
questions.explanation: Cropping intensity = gross cropped area/net cultivated area × 100. Three full-hectare crops give 3 ha-crops/1 ha × 100 = 300%.
optionExplanations: 100% represents one full crop per year.
200% represents two full crops.
Correct. Three full crops equal 300% intensity.
600% would require six full crop cycles.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Vegetables are transplanted at 0.25 m × 0.25 m spacing. Approximately how many planting positions fit in one hectare?
questions.explanation: Area per position = 0.0625 m²; 10,000/0.0625 = 160,000 positions/ha.
optionExplanations: This is one tenth of the correct value.
This corresponds to much wider spacing.
This is half the correct value.
Correct. 160,000 positions/ha.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A 20 m² harvest plot yields 12 kg of marketable produce. The equivalent yield is:
questions.explanation: 12 kg/20 m² = 0.6 kg/m². Multiply by 10,000 m²/ha = 6,000 kg/ha = 6 t/ha.
optionExplanations: 0.6 t/ha misses a factor of ten.
3.0 t/ha is half the correct conversion.
Correct. The equivalent is 6 t/ha.
12 t/ha doubles the result.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A farmer needs 100 kg/ha of viable seed, but a seed lot has only 80% germination and purity is assumed 100%. What seed rate approximately compensates for germination?
questions.explanation: Adjusted seed rate = desired viable seed ÷ germination fraction = 100/0.80 = 125 kg/ha.
optionExplanations: Using less seed worsens the shortfall.
This assumes 100% germination.
Correct. 100 ÷ 0.80 = 125 kg/ha.
180 kg/ha overcompensates.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: A short-day plant receives a brief red-light interruption in the middle of a long night. What is the most likely effect?
options: Flowering may be inhibited because the long dark period was interrupted
Flowering is guaranteed regardless of photoperiod
The plant becomes a C4 species
questions.explanation: For many short-day plants, an uninterrupted long night is critical; a night break can inhibit floral induction.
optionExplanations: Correct. Night interruption can prevent the required long dark period.
Photoperiodic flowering remains conditional.
Photosynthetic pathway does not change this way.
Night interruption does not permanently remove seed dormancy.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: Why are nursery seedlings commonly hardened before transplanting to the field?
options: To gradually increase tolerance to field stresses and reduce transplant shock
To force immediate flowering in every crop
questions.explanation: Hardening exposes seedlings gradually to lower water availability, stronger light, temperature variation, or reduced fertilizer so they withstand transplant stress.
optionExplanations: Correct. Hardening improves stress tolerance during establishment.
Hardening is not a breeding method.
It does not sterilize soil.
It does not universally force flowering.

questions.subject: Crop Science
questions.question: During grain filling, severe defoliation most directly reduces yield because it:
options: Reduces photosynthetic source capacity supplying assimilates to developing grains
questions.explanation: Leaves are major sources of assimilates. Severe defoliation during grain filling reduces carbohydrate supply to grain sinks.
optionExplanations: Correct. Less source capacity can limit grain filling.
Defoliation decreases, not increases, leaf area.
Grains do not convert into roots.
Mineral uptake may continue; the direct effect is reduced assimilate supply.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: In a field sample, 24 of 120 plants show a disease. Disease incidence is:
questions.explanation: Disease incidence = diseased units/total units × 100 = 24/120 × 100 = 20%.
optionExplanations: 10% understates the fraction.
24 is the number diseased, not the percentage.
80% is the healthy proportion.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: A label rate is 2 mL of product per liter of spray water. How much product is needed for a 200-L tank?
questions.explanation: Product required = 2 mL/L × 200 L = 400 mL.
optionExplanations: 100 mL would be 0.5 mL/L.
200 mL would be 1 mL/L.
Correct. 2 × 200 = 400 mL.
2,000 mL would be 10 mL/L.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: You need 100 g active ingredient from a 50% wettable powder. How much formulated product is required?
questions.explanation: Product amount = required active ingredient / fraction active ingredient = 100/0.50 = 200 g.
optionExplanations: 50 g supplies only 25 g active ingredient.
100 g supplies 50 g active ingredient.
Correct. 200 g of 50% product supplies 100 g a.i.
500 g supplies 250 g active ingredient.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Using EIL = C/(V×I×D×K), let control cost C=₱600/ha, crop value V=₱30/kg, injury per pest I=0.2 units, damage per injury D=0.5 kg, and control effectiveness K=0.5. What is the EIL?
optionExplanations: 40 is ten times too low.
200 is half the correct result.
Correct. EIL = 400 pests/ha.
800 doubles the calculated value.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Scouting shows a pest population below the economic threshold and abundant natural enemies. The best IPM decision is usually to:
options: Apply the maximum insecticide dose immediately
Continue monitoring and conserve natural enemies
Stop scouting for the rest of the season
questions.explanation: Below-threshold populations usually do not justify disruptive control; monitoring should continue because populations can change.
optionExplanations: Routine high-dose spraying conflicts with threshold-based IPM.
Correct. Monitor and preserve biological control.
Beneficial insects help suppress pests.
Scouting should continue.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: For a contact protectant fungicide, the most effective timing is generally:
options: Before infection or before a forecast infection period
Only after tissue is completely destroyed
When no susceptible tissue is present
questions.explanation: Protectants work on treated surfaces to prevent infection, so coverage before infection is crucial.
optionExplanations: Correct. Preventive coverage is the key.
Destroyed tissue cannot be restored by a protectant.
Postharvest timing does not protect the standing crop.
No susceptible tissue means little protective value.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Which spray program best slows evolution of fungicide resistance?
options: Repeated use of the same single-site mode of action
Rotate or mix effective modes of action according to resistance-management guidance
Increase dose above the label each week
questions.explanation: Reducing repeated selection by one target-site mode and integrating nonchemical measures helps slow resistance.
optionExplanations: Repeated single-mode use strongly selects resistant strains.
Correct. Mode-of-action stewardship reduces selection pressure.
Above-label rates are unsafe and do not guarantee resistance prevention.
Unnecessary spraying adds selection pressure.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: A preemergence herbicide is normally applied:
options: Before weed seedlings emerge, often near planting
Directly into irrigation pumps regardless of label
questions.explanation: Preemergence herbicides act before weeds emerge or during very early germination, depending on the product label.
optionExplanations: Correct. Timing is before emergence of target weeds.
Seed production is far too late.
Harvested grain is not the target.
Application must follow the label.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Chewing mouthparts most commonly produce which symptom?
options: Holes, notches, or missing leaf tissue
Uniform interveinal chlorosis without tissue loss
questions.explanation: Chewing insects physically remove plant tissue, producing holes, notches, skeletonization, or defoliation.
optionExplanations: Correct. Tissue removal is characteristic of chewing.
Chlorosis can have many nutritional or sucking-pest causes.
Root knots are caused by root-knot nematodes.
Viruses may cause mosaics but the symptom is not itself chewing damage.

questions.subject: Crop Protection
questions.question: Why should pruning tools be disinfected between plants when managing a mechanically transmissible bacterial disease?
options: To reduce transfer of inoculum on contaminated tools
questions.explanation: Contaminated cutting tools can carry bacterial inoculum from infected to healthy plants.
optionExplanations: Correct. Disinfection interrupts mechanical transmission.
Tool disinfection does not increase pollination.
It does not alter soil pH.
It cannot change host genotype.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A mineral soil has bulk density 1.325 g/cm³ and particle density 2.65 g/cm³. Approximate total porosity is:
questions.explanation: Porosity = [1 − (bulk density/particle density)] × 100 = [1 − 1.325/2.65]×100 = 50%.
optionExplanations: 25% is too low.
40% does not match the density ratio.
Correct. The bulk density is one-half the particle density, giving 50% pore space.
75% would require a much lower bulk density.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A crop requires 90 kg N/ha. Approximately how much 46-0-0 urea supplies this nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Urea required = 90/0.46 ≈ 195.7 kg/ha.
optionExplanations: 41.4 kg is 46% of 90, not fertilizer required.
90 kg urea supplies only 41.4 kg N.
414 kg would supply about 190 kg N.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: How much 14-14-14 fertilizer is required to supply 42 kg N/ha?
questions.explanation: Fertilizer required = 42/0.14 = 300 kg/ha. This also supplies 42 kg P₂O₅ and 42 kg K₂O.
optionExplanations: 42 kg supplies only 5.88 kg N.
140 kg supplies 19.6 kg N.
Correct. 300 kg × 0.14 = 42 kg N.
420 kg supplies 58.8 kg N.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil pH of 5.0 is best described as:
options: Strongly acidic relative to neutral pH 7
questions.explanation: pH 5 is acidic; salinity is a separate property measured with electrical conductivity or related indices.
optionExplanations: Correct. It is distinctly acidic.
Neutral soil is near pH 7.
Alkaline soils have pH above 7.
pH alone does not define salinity.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil has field capacity of 30% and permanent wilting point of 15% on the same water-content basis. Available water capacity is:
questions.explanation: Available water = field capacity − permanent wilting point = 30 − 15 = 15 percentage points.
optionExplanations: Correct. The difference is 15.
This uses field capacity alone.
This incorrectly adds the two values.
No calculation gives 50.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A moist soil sample weighs 130 g and weighs 100 g after oven drying. Gravimetric water content is:
questions.explanation: Gravimetric water content = (wet mass − dry mass)/dry mass ×100 = 30/100×100 = 30%.
optionExplanations: 23.1% uses wet mass in the denominator.
Correct. Water mass is 30 g relative to 100 g dry soil.
76.9% is unrelated.
130% is the wet/dry ratio rather than water content.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: If the root zone is 0.30 m deep and volumetric water content must increase by 0.10 m³/m³, the net water depth required is approximately:
questions.explanation: Water depth = change in volumetric content × root-zone depth = 0.10×0.30 m = 0.03 m = 30 mm.
optionExplanations: 3 mm is one tenth of the required depth.
Correct. 0.03 m equals 30 mm.
100 mm is too large.
300 mm equals the full root-zone depth.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil has exchangeable Ca=10, Mg=4, K=1, and Na=1 cmolc/kg, with negligible exchangeable acidity. Approximate CEC is:
questions.explanation: With negligible acidity, CEC is approximately the sum of exchangeable cations: 10+4+1+1=16 cmolc/kg.
optionExplanations: 4 includes only Mg.
8 is not the sum.
Correct. Sum = 16 cmolc/kg.
20 would require additional charge not given.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: Exchangeable base cations total 16 cmolc/kg and CEC is 20 cmolc/kg. Base saturation is:
questions.explanation: Base saturation = sum of exchangeable bases/CEC ×100 = 16/20×100 = 80%.
optionExplanations: 20% confuses CEC with percentage.
40% is half the correct ratio.
Correct. 80% of exchange sites are occupied by bases.
Base saturation should not exceed 100% under this definition.

questions.subject: Soil Science
questions.question: A soil containing about 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay is most consistent with which broad USDA textural class?
questions.explanation: A balanced mixture around 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay falls in the loam region of the texture triangle.
optionExplanations: Correct. This mixture is characteristic of loam.
Sand would require much higher sand content.
Clay requires substantially higher clay content.
Silt requires much higher silt content.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A group of pigs consumes 3,600 kg feed and gains 2,000 kg live weight. Feed conversion ratio is:
questions.explanation: FCR = feed consumed/weight gain = 3,600/2,000 = 1.80.
optionExplanations: 0.56 is approximately the reciprocal.
Correct. FCR is 1.80.
2.00 is too high for the given numbers.
5.60 is unrelated.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A calf increases from 180 kg to 240 kg over 60 days. Average daily gain is:
optionExplanations: 0.5 kg/day would give only 30 kg gain.
Correct. The calf gained 1 kg per day.
2 kg/day would give 120 kg gain.
4 kg/day is four times the calculated rate.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A hog has a live weight of 100 kg and hot carcass weight of 75 kg. Dressing percentage is:
questions.explanation: Dressing percentage = carcass/live ×100 = 75/100×100 = 75%.
optionExplanations: 25% is not the carcass proportion.
50% understates carcass yield.
Correct. Dressing percentage is 75%.
133% is the inverse ratio.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A flock begins with 1,000 birds and 40 die during the production cycle. Mortality rate is:
questions.explanation: Mortality = deaths/initial population ×100 = 40/1000×100 = 4%.
optionExplanations: 0.4% is ten times too low.
Correct. 40 of 1,000 is 4%.
40% would mean 400 deaths.
96% is the survival percentage.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Out of 80 inseminated cows, 48 are confirmed pregnant. Conception rate is:
questions.explanation: Conception rate = pregnant/inseminated ×100 = 48/80×100 = 60%.
optionExplanations: 40% is the nonpregnant proportion.
48 is the number pregnant, not the rate.
Correct. 60%.
80 is the number inseminated.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A 100-kg feed batch contains 20 kg crude protein equivalent. Crude protein concentration is:
questions.explanation: Crude protein percent = 20/100×100 = 20%.
optionExplanations: 2% would mean only 2 kg CP.
Correct. 20 kg per 100 kg is 20%.
50% would require 50 kg CP.
80% would require 80 kg CP.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Ten dairy cows produce a total of 180 liters of milk in one day. Average daily milk yield per cow is:
questions.explanation: Average = 180 L/10 cows = 18 L/cow/day.
optionExplanations: 9 L is half the average.
Correct. 18 liters per cow.
90 L is five times too high.
180 L is the herd total.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: A pen has 60 m² usable floor area for 30 animals. Stocking space is:
questions.explanation: Space allowance = area/animals = 60/30 = 2 m² per animal.
optionExplanations: 0.5 is the inverse-style error.
1 m² would require 30 m² total.
Correct. Each animal has 2 m².
30 m² each would require 900 m².

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: From 500 fertile eggs set, 400 chicks hatch. Hatchability of fertile eggs is:
questions.explanation: Hatchability = chicks hatched/fertile eggs set ×100 = 400/500×100 = 80%.
optionExplanations: 20% is the failure rate.
50% is too low.
Correct. 80% hatchability.
A hatchability above 100% is impossible.

questions.subject: Animal Science
questions.question: Why is timely colostrum intake especially important for newborn calves?
options: It supplies immunoglobulins before intestinal absorption of large antibodies declines
It permanently replaces all future vaccinations
It prevents the rumen from ever developing
It provides no nutrients but only water
questions.explanation: Colostrum supplies antibodies, energy, vitamins, and other protective factors; passive antibody absorption is greatest soon after birth.
optionExplanations: Correct. Early intake maximizes passive immunity.
Vaccination and disease prevention are still needed later.
Rumen development proceeds normally with age and diet.
Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not just water.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Fixed cost is ₱30,000, selling price ₱80/unit, and variable cost ₱50/unit. Break-even output is:
questions.explanation: Contribution margin = 80−50 = ₱30. Break-even quantity = 30,000/30 = 1,000 units.
optionExplanations: 375 divides fixed cost by price.
600 divides fixed cost by variable cost.
Correct. 1,000 units.
1,500 would require a ₱20 contribution margin.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: A vegetable enterprise earns ₱150,000 gross revenue and incurs ₱90,000 variable costs. Gross margin is:
questions.explanation: Gross margin = gross revenue − variable cost = 150,000−90,000 = ₱60,000.
optionExplanations: Correct. ₱60,000.
This is variable cost, not margin.
This is gross revenue.
This adds rather than subtracts.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Gross farm income is ₱500,000, variable costs are ₱280,000, and fixed costs are ₱120,000. Net farm income is:
optionExplanations: Correct. ₱100,000 remains after both cost classes.
₱220,000 subtracts only variable costs.
₱380,000 subtracts only fixed costs.
₱900,000 adds costs to income.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: An enterprise earns ₱25,000 net profit on ₱100,000 total investment. Simple ROI is:
questions.explanation: ROI = net profit/investment ×100 = 25,000/100,000×100 = 25%.
optionExplanations: 4% is the inverse-scale error.
20% does not match the ratio.
Correct. ROI = 25%.
400% is the inverse percentage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Present value of benefits is ₱240,000 and present value of costs is ₱160,000. BCR is:
questions.explanation: BCR = benefits/costs = 240,000/160,000 = 1.5.
optionExplanations: 0.67 is the inverse.
1.0 would mean equal benefits and costs.
Correct. BCR=1.5.
80 is not a ratio from these values.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%. Using the simple percentage approach, price elasticity of demand is approximately:
questions.explanation: Elasticity = %ΔQ/%ΔP = −20%/+10% = −2. Demand is elastic in absolute value.
optionExplanations: −0.5 reverses numerator and denominator.
−1.0 would be unit elastic.
Correct. −2.0.
The usual own-price relationship gives a negative sign.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: A retailer sells produce for ₱80/kg after buying it from a wholesaler at ₱60/kg. The retailer’s gross marketing margin is:
questions.explanation: Margin between these stages = selling price−purchase price = 80−60 = ₱20/kg.
optionExplanations: Correct. ₱20/kg.
₱60 is the purchase price.
₱80 is the retail price.
₱140 adds the two prices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: Consumers pay ₱100/kg while farmers receive ₱55/kg. The farm-to-retail price spread is:
questions.explanation: Price spread = consumer price−farm price = 100−55 = ₱45/kg.
optionExplanations: Correct. ₱45/kg.
₱55 is the farmgate price.
₱100 is the retail price.
₱155 adds instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: A machine costs ₱120,000, has ₱20,000 salvage value, and a 5-year useful life. Straight-line annual depreciation is:
optionExplanations: ₱4,000 incorrectly divides salvage value by life.
Correct. ₱20,000 per year.
₱24,000 ignores salvage value.
₱100,000 is the total depreciable amount, not annual depreciation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Economics & Marketing
questions.question: A farmer borrows ₱50,000 at 8% simple annual interest for one year. Interest due is:
questions.explanation: Simple interest = principal×rate×time = 50,000×0.08×1 = ₱4,000.
optionExplanations: Correct. ₱4,000.
₱8,000 would correspond to 16%.
₱54,000 is principal plus interest, not interest alone.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: A program targets 200 farmers and 120 are verified to have adopted the recommended practice. Adoption rate is:
questions.explanation: Adoption rate = adopters/target group ×100 = 120/200×100 = 60%.
optionExplanations: 40% is the non-adopter percentage.
Correct. 60%.
80% would require 160 adopters.
Rates cannot exceed 100% here.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: A training invited 150 farmers and 105 attended. Attendance rate is:
optionExplanations: 30% is the nonattendance proportion.
45% is too low.
Correct. 70%.
105 is the number attending, not the percentage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Average pretest score is 55% and average posttest score is 80%. The percentage-point gain is:
questions.explanation: Percentage-point gain = 80−55 = 25 points.
optionExplanations: Correct. The gain is 25 percentage points.
35 is not the difference.
45 is not the difference.
Scores do not add for gain.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: An extension survey is sent to 250 farmers and 175 usable responses are returned. Response rate is:
questions.explanation: Response rate = 175/250×100 = 70%.
optionExplanations: 30% is the nonresponse percentage.
57% is incorrect.
Correct. 70%.
A response rate above 100% is not possible.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Farmers need to learn the exact steps for calibrating a backpack sprayer. Which method is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A method demonstration is specifically designed to teach how to perform a skill step by step.
optionExplanations: Correct. It teaches the procedure directly.
Result demonstrations emphasize outcomes or benefits.
Radio may create awareness but is weak for hands-on calibration skill.
A poster alone lacks guided practice.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: A farmer group doubts whether a new variety performs better under local conditions. Which approach best addresses this concern?
options: A local result demonstration comparing performance
A method demonstration on knot tying
questions.explanation: A result demonstration shows the practical outcome of a recommended practice or technology under conditions meaningful to farmers.
optionExplanations: Correct. Local visible results address performance doubts.
Unrelated history does not test the claim.
Knot tying is unrelated to variety performance.
Evidence helps informed evaluation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: An extension worker explains a technical term, but farmers interpret it differently because of unfamiliar jargon. This is primarily:
questions.explanation: Semantic noise arises when words, symbols, or meanings are not shared or are misunderstood.
optionExplanations: Correct. Jargon can create semantic interference.
Physical noise involves environmental sound or signal interference.
Feedback is a response, not the misunderstanding itself.
Trialability is an innovation attribute.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Before designing a livelihood training, the extension team conducts interviews, mapping, and group discussions to identify priority problems. This is mainly:
questions.explanation: Needs assessment identifies current conditions, gaps, priorities, resources, and stakeholder perspectives before program design.
optionExplanations: Correct. Diagnosis should precede intervention design.
Impact evaluation occurs after implementation has produced outcomes.
Product pricing is a marketing task.
Random promotion is not systematic planning.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: Which is the best SMART-style extension objective?
options: By December, at least 70% of 100 trained growers will correctly calibrate a knapsack sprayer using the recommended procedure
Improve agriculture as much as possible
questions.explanation: The first objective specifies who, how many, what behavior, and by when, making it measurable and time-bound.
optionExplanations: Correct. It is specific, measurable, attainable/relevant in context, and time-bound.
“Understand” and “someday” are vague.
This states an activity without a measurable learner outcome.
This is too broad to evaluate.

questions.subject: Agricultural Extension & Communication
questions.question: In a program logic model, “50 farmers completed a two-day training” is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: Outputs are immediate products of activities, such as people trained, demonstrations conducted, or materials distributed.
optionExplanations: Correct. Number trained is an output.
Long-term impact concerns broader sustained change.
Inputs are resources such as staff, funds, and materials.
An assumption is a condition believed necessary for the logic to hold.
